title: Retrieve stated evidence
summary: Locate the exact part of a passage that answers a question, then paraphrase it without changing the stated facts, scope or limitations.

sections.title: Answer what the passage states
content: A stated-evidence question can be proved with words already present in the passage. Your task is to find the relevant statement and express it accurately, not to add a likely explanation.
Before searching, underline the question word and the exact target: who, what, when, where, why, how, how many, or which limitation.

sections.title: Use Locate, Link and Prove
content: Locate: turn the question into search terms and scan for the same idea, including synonyms rather than only repeated words.
Link: read the complete sentence and at least one sentence around it. Match pronouns, causes, comparisons and sequence to the question's target.
Prove: point to the smallest sufficient evidence span. If the answer needs two details, confirm that both are explicitly stated before responding.

sections.title: Paraphrase without changing the claim
content: Example statement: “Rain days were excluded because wet surfaces become temporarily cooler.” Question: Why did the team omit readings from rainy days? Accurate answer: Wet surfaces would temporarily lower the readings and distort the comparison.
The paraphrase changes the wording but preserves the actor, cause and degree of certainty. It does not invent a broken sensor, unsafe weather or a permanent cooling effect.
Keep exact numbers, time periods, names and limiting words such as only, average, may, could not prove and rather than.

sections.title: Build a fact frame
content: Write a compact frame before answering: actor + action or finding + required condition. For a why question, add the stated cause; for a comparison, add both sides and the measurement.
Cross out nearby facts that answer a different question. A detail can be true in the passage and still be irrelevant to the target.

sections.title: Retrieve across a complete report
content: Move from the question to the likely paragraph using the passage map, then scan within that paragraph. Return to the surrounding sentences when the answer contains a reason, contrast or qualification.
For multiple-response items, test every option against a specific line. Select an option only when all of its important details are stated.

sections.title: Diagnose evidence drift
content: Wrong target: I found a related fact but answered a different question.
Incomplete evidence: I omitted a required reason, comparison, number or limitation.
Meaning drift: my paraphrase changed who did the action, the strength of the claim or the time period.
Inference added: I supplied a plausible idea that the writer never stated. Record one cause before correcting the answer.

sections.title: A cooler route to school
content: Retrieve six sets of stated evidence from an original five-paragraph report. All responses are marked together so the passage remains a complete reading task.
